spec_choices.why: The designer's suggested size is 3 and the source allows 3 to 4. The minimum is 3 because with 2 players a respondent sees only the asker's rack, so answers reveal it almost directly. The maximum stays at 4, as in the source; more racks per question would make answers too diluted and turns too slow.

A thoughtful player picks questions and respondents whose answers best split the possible racks they could hold, uses the public discard and the tile counts, notes what the questions reveal to opponents, and passes until confident, because a wrong guess costs a point.
The source explicitly has none; the engine-answered questions are the only shared information.

spec_choices.what: Question and respondent combined into one choice, with k asked in a separate step only for NUMBER
spec_choices.why: It fits the engine's choice-from-a-list answer type while keeping the active player's single decision.

spec_choices.what: An unparseable guess is treated as PASS
spec_choices.why: The source does not cover malformed answers; PASS is the neutral reading.

spec_choices.what: When the deck is replenished, the whole discard pile moves into the deck
spec_choices.why: The source says the discard pile is shuffled in; drawing at random makes an explicit shuffle unnecessary.

simplifications.what: The guess is free text parsed into three numbers rather than a menu of all 84 multisets
simplifications.why: This avoids an oversized option list.

simplifications.what: The two ways the game can end share one ranking (highest score; ties share the win)
simplifications.why: The source decides the winner the same way for both endings, and the engine treats a shared top as a draw.

variation.original_summary: Code 777 is a deduction game for 2 to 5 players. Each player sees everyone's number tiles except their own three. Players take turns drawing a question card and answering it publicly from what they see. Anyone may interrupt at any moment to guess their own three numbers: a correct guess scores 1 point, and the first player to 3 points wins.

review.evidence: Deduction drives results, but the free interrupt makes speed of shouting matter. A wrong guess costs nothing in points: it only resets your rack, which can even replace a hard rack with an easy one. A spam-guess policy is therefore cheap. Always-pass scores 0 and loses, which is fine.

Good deducers win more often. However, which question card comes up, and therefore who it helps, is pure luck. Freshly dealt racks vary a lot in how easy they are to deduce (a rack holding the single 1 is far easier). Real-time reflexes also decide close races.

Weak players still deduce something from obvious answers. Strong players combine every public answer with tile-supply counting (one 1, two 2s, up to seven 7s) and discarded tiles, and they judge the right moment to risk a guess.
The core is inference about a hidden state, your own rack. You reason from other players' answers, which describe a view that includes your rack and excludes theirs.
Guesses are right or wrong and points are counted. The only soft spot is that players answer questions themselves and could err; an engine can compute the answers instead.

Interrupting at any time is real-time play, which the engine does not support. The random question deck plus random tile replacement is two chance events per turn. Colors double the tracked state (number plus color for every tile), which overflows the attribute limit with 4 players.

problems: P1: Guessing by interrupt at any moment is real-time, which the engine does not support, and it rewards speed rather than reasoning.
P2: A wrong guess costs no points, so blind or premature guessing is nearly free, and resetting your rack can even help.
P3: A random question deck decides what information appears and whom it helps. That is luck, and a second chance event each turn, together with tile replacement.
P4: Players have no strategic choice in what to ask, so there is little opponent modelling beyond the race to guess.
P5: Tracking colors as well as numbers for every tile exceeds the attribute limit with 4 players and lengthens every question.
P6: There is no length cap; a game where nobody reaches 3 could run indefinitely.

changes.what: Replace interrupts with a simultaneous guess poll at the end of every round: each player either guesses their three numbers or passes.
changes.why: It is turn-based and removes the reflex advantage; every player gets the same chance to act on the same information.

changes.what: A wrong guess costs 1 point, and scores may go negative. Your rack is still replaced after any guess, right or wrong.
changes.why: Guessing becomes a calculated risk, so you guess only once your deduction is confident. The always-guess policy now sinks below zero.

changes.what: Drop the question deck. The active player picks a question from a fixed menu of six, and names which other player (the respondent) must have the engine answer it from that player's point of view.
changes.why: This removes the luck of the question draw and leaves only one chance event per round, the tile replacement. Choosing the question means steering the information toward your own rack. Choosing the respondent means denying information to the leader, because the respondent learns nothing about their own rack from their own answer. Both choices take planning and opponent modelling.

changes.what: The engine computes every answer exactly from the tiles.
changes.why: Answers are verifiable and cannot be lied about or miscounted.

changes.what: The asker's choice of question and respondent is a deliberate strategic act, as described above.
changes.why: Every turn becomes a decision about which information to release and to whom.

changes.what: Remove colors. Tiles are numbers only, and the menu uses number properties instead (even, high, specific number, rack sum, pairs, missing numbers).
changes.why: It keeps state within 20 attributes for 4 players and keeps every question a simple count.

changes.what: Cap the game at 10 rounds per player (30 rounds with 3 players, 40 with 4). The first player to 3 points wins. At the cap, the highest score wins.
changes.why: This bounds the length. Each seat asks equally often, so asking first is not an edge.

keeps: You see every rack except your own and must deduce your own three numbers.
The 28-tile pool of one 1, two 2s, through seven 7s, so supply counting is a deduction tool.
Public questions answered from one player's view, which tell everyone else about their own racks.
Guess your exact three numbers to score 1 point; your rack is then replaced from the pile.

recommendation.reason: The hidden-own-rack deduction is an excellent fit for reasoning training. Its unsupported parts (real-time interrupts, a random question deck, colors) can be replaced by a turn-based ask-and-guess loop that adds strategic question selection and keeps the game's identity.

variation.name: Code 777: Ask and Guess
variation.summary: Each player sees everyone's tiles but their own. Each turn the active player chooses a question and a respondent, the engine answers it publicly from the respondent's view, and then everyone may risk a guess at their own three numbers. First to 3 points wins.
variation.rules:
TILES. There are 28 tiles: one 1, two 2s, three 3s, four 4s, five 5s, six 6s and seven 7s.

SETUP. Shuffle the tiles into a face-down pile. Deal 3 tiles to each player's rack. Each player is told privately the numbers on every OTHER player's rack, but never their own. Each player starts with 0 points. The discard pile starts empty and is public: everyone always sees which tiles are in it. Seats are numbered 1 to N. Seat 1 is the active player in round 1, and the active player then rotates in seat order each round.

EACH ROUND:
1. The engine announces the round number and the active player.
2. The active player makes one choice: a question from the menu below, and a respondent, who must be one other player. For question 3, the active player also names a number k from 1 to 7.
3. The engine computes the answer exactly, counting only the tiles the respondent can see: every rack except the respondent's own. This includes the active player's rack. The engine announces the question, the respondent and the answer to everyone.
   Menu:
   (1) EVEN: how many even tiles (2, 4, 6) do you see?
   (2) HIGH: how many tiles numbered 5, 6 or 7 do you see?
   (3) NUMBER k: how many tiles numbered k do you see?
   (4) SUM15: how many of the racks you see total 15 or more?
   (5) PAIR: how many of the racks you see hold at least two tiles of the same number?
   (6) MISSING: how many of the numbers 1 to 7 appear on none of the racks you see?
4. GUESS POLL. All players answer at the same moment, without seeing each other's answers. Each either writes PASS or writes three numbers (order irrelevant) as a guess at their own rack.
5. SCORING. A guess that matches the player's rack exactly as a set of three numbers, duplicates included, scores +1 point. Any other guess scores -1 point. PASS scores 0. Scores may be negative.
6. REVEAL AND REPLACE. Every player who guessed, right or wrong, has their three tiles announced to all and moved to the discard pile. If the face-down pile then holds fewer tiles than are needed, the discard pile is shuffled into it. The engine then deals 3 new tiles to each player who guessed. This is the round's single random event.
7. Every player is privately told the current racks of all OTHER players.
8. END CHECK. If any player has 3 or more points, the game ends. Otherwise, if the final round has been played, the game ends. The final round is round 30 with 3 players and round 40 with 4 players.

There is no talk phase; the engine-answered questions are the only shared information.
variation.objective: When the game ends because someone reached 3 points, the player with the most points wins. If two or more players share that top score, the game is a draw. If the round limit is reached instead, the player with the highest score wins, and a tie for the highest score is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Players must combine public answers, tile-supply counting and the public discard pile to narrow their own rack, then judge when to guess. The -1 penalty punishes impatience, and always-guess goes deeply negative. Always-pass scores 0 and loses to anyone who scores. Every question informs all players except the respondent, so the asker must pick a question that pins down their own rack while naming as respondent the opponent who is closest to a guess, denying them that information. Simultaneous guessing removes reflexes. Rotating askers with 10 asks each balances the seats. Many rack replacements over a game average out easy and hard deals. Talk is omitted: the only thing players could usefully say is (possibly false) statements about other players' racks, which would replace deduction with kingmaking and noise rather than add a real decision.

balanced.evidence:
WHO LEARNS WHAT. An answer counts every rack except the respondent's. The active player and every other non-respondent see all of those racks except their own. So each of them can subtract and learn an exact fact about their own rack: a count of evens, highs or k's, or whether their rack sums to 15+ or holds a pair. The respondent learns nothing new, because they already see every rack counted. Every question therefore informs all players except the respondent.

PAYOFF PER GUESS. A guess right with probability p is worth 2p-1. It is worth +1 at p=1, 0 at p=0.5 and -1 at p=0. PASS is worth 0. Guess only above p=0.5.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES (3-player example: 28-6=22 unseen tiles, own 3 among them, C(22,3)=1540 possible sets):
- Always guess the most likely set from the opening prior. The best set {7,7,6} has P = 21*6/1540 = 0.082. EV is about -0.84 per round, falling to roughly -25 over 30 rounds. Against any opponent who ever scores (sensible, or random who occasionally hits), it loses nearly always. Against an always-PASS opponent it is at a net negative score, so it trails 0 and loses. It never wins or draws.
- Always guess at random: P(correct) is under 0.08 per guess. It loses to sensible play and to always-PASS, which stays at 0.
- Always PASS: score stays 0. It loses to any sensible player, who deduces a rack within a few questions and scores +1 each time. Against a random guesser it wins, because that player goes negative. That is not the 'never loses' failure, since it loses to sensible play almost always.
- Always choose question 1, or always the first respondent: this only gives weaker information or targets a fixed rival. It does not beat varied question choice.
- No question or guess option is strictly dominant.

DEDUCTION NEEDS SEVERAL ROUNDS. After NUMBER 7 reports two 7s, the third tile is the most common remaining number with p of about 6/20 = 0.3. That is still below 0.5, so further questions are needed before guessing.

SEATS. Rotation gives each seat exactly 10 turns as active player in 30 rounds (3 players) or 40 rounds (4 players). Seat 1's only edge is asking first and having had more active turns if the game ends early at 3 points; this is minor.
- The active player's edge is real but fair: they can tailor the question to their own uncertainty. They can also deny information to a leader by naming that leader as respondent, which is genuine opponent modelling.
- Information is symmetric, because the guess poll is simultaneous after a public answer.

CAN EVERYONE WIN? Yes. Each player needs three correct deductions. The fixed-length 'safe option' trap does not apply: PASS never wins against sensible play, and there is no cooperation to betray.

playable.evidence:
RULES ARE COMPLETE.
- Tile counts are given: 1 to 7 copies of each number, 28 in all.
- The deal, private views, public discard pile and active-player rotation are defined.
- The respondent must be another player. k is required only for question 3.
- The scoring set-match includes duplicates.
- Reshuffling when the pile runs low is defined, and there are always enough tiles: at most 12 on racks out of 28.
- The end check and tie-is-a-draw cases are defined.

FINITE. The game lasts at most 30 or 40 rounds, or ends early at 3 points. The winner is decided by arithmetic on stored scores.

LIMITS. All within limits as stated:
- steps 12 of 20;
- choice steps 2 of 4 (a question+respondent choice, then a simultaneous guess poll);
- attributes 19 of 20 (12 rack slots, 4 scores, pile, discard, round);
- hidden elements 2 of 3 (own rack, pile order);
- 1 random event per round (the shuffle-if-needed plus deal);
- rounds 40 of 40.

NEEDS NOTHING THE ENGINE LACKS. There is no board, judge or clock. Private values, simultaneous choice and a shared deck via list operations are all supported.

CAVEAT. Computing an answer 'excluding the respondent' with a variable respondent needs the player-attribute workaround: compute the total over all racks, then subtract the respondent's rack with an if per seat. MISSING needs a per-number presence calc. This fits in calc steps but is the tightest part of the step budget; it is feasible.

TALK. Omitting talk is sensible. The only interaction is the active player's choice of question and respondent; it is not a coordination or bargaining problem. Talk could only be unenforceable requests or bluffs about one's own uncertainty, which add words but no decision that following a proposal makes costly. Players are not reduced to blind guessing about each other, because the public answers carry the information.

triage.reason: The game legitimately combines the question and the respondent into one choice, offering options like 'EVEN to seat 2', which fits the rule that the active player makes one choice of question plus respondent. The tests look for a bare option named 'EVEN', 'HIGH' or 'NUMBER' that the rules never prescribe, so their rules never matched and the follow-up steps (such as naming k) were never reached.
triage.guidance:
Do not assume the exact option strings. The interface fixes attribute names, not option labels.
- **Matching question options:** match by content, either an option containing the question name (e.g. 'EVEN') or the full combined form 'EVEN to seat 2'.
- **Respondent rule:** check that seat 1 is never offered any option naming seat 1 as respondent.
- **Active seat:** check that only the active seat gets question options, using containment matching. In round 2, seat 2's options should name seats 1 and 3.
- **NUMBER test:** first pick an option containing 'NUMBER'. Then expect a follow-up choice offering k from 1 to 7, matched by value.
- **Answer checks:** where possible, assert on the public `answer` and on scores rather than on option text.

triage.reason: The rules call the active player's question and respondent one choice. The game offers combined options such as 'EVEN to seat 2' and 'EVEN to seat 3', which follows the rules. The tests look for a bare option string 'EVEN', and 'k' values offered as separate options, which this faithful encoding never produces. The NUMBER scenario also expects an exact answer of 2 that depends on which tiles the shuffle deals, so chance decides it, not the rules.
triage.guidance:
Match options by content, not exact label. An option whose text starts with or contains the question name and a respondent seat (for example 'EVEN to seat 2') satisfies 'question offered'.
- For R4: check that seat 1 in round 1 and seat 2 in round 2 get question options, and that the other seats get only the guess poll.
- For R5: check that no offered option names the active seat itself as respondent (seat 1 sees only 'to seat 2' and 'to seat 3').
- For R6: accept k being folded into the option (for example 'NUMBER 5 to seat 2') or asked in a follow-up step. Check that the values 1 through 7 are all available, in whatever form the game offers them.
- Do not assert an exact answer that depends on the random deal. Either compute the expected answer from the racks the game actually dealt in that run (the respondent's view: all racks except its own), or assert only that the answer is a number between 0 and 3N - 3.

triage.reason: The game deals racks and keeps the deck at 28 - 3N: the trace shows 19 tiles in the deck after two all-pass rounds with 3 players, scores at 0 and an empty discard. It offers the active player one combined choice of question and respondent, labelled like 'EVEN to seat 2'. Every failure is the test's rule `options_include: "EVEN"` never matching, because no option is labelled exactly 'EVEN'.
triage.guidance: Match the active player's option by its real label: the rules make question and respondent a single choice, so the game offers labels such as 'EVEN to seat 2' or 'EVEN to seat 1'. Either name the full option ('EVEN to seat 2' for seat 1 in round 1) or match by prefix or substring rather than an exact 'EVEN'. In the setup and R2/R3 scenarios, the simplest fix is to let seat 1 play an all-PASS-safe question, or drop the option rule altogether, since those scenarios only check rack sizes, deck size, scores and discard. Keep the lens checks (deck 19 or 16, racks of 3, discard empty, scores 0), which the game already satisfies.
